title: Missing Security Rate-Limiting Controls Leading to Credential Brute-Forcing
category: A09 - Security Logging and Alerting Failures
description: The login authentication interface fails to restrict high-speed, automated credential submission traffic. By routing authentication attempts through Burp Intruder, an attacker can continuously test password lists against server endpoints without triggering security blocks, captchas, account locks, or logging restriction boundaries.
impact: The complete absence of rate-limiting infrastructure lets attackers execute brute-force and credential-stuffing scripts indefinitely. Because these high-velocity events do not activate defensive alerts or threshold bans, accounts can be compromised over time without alerting security monitoring operators.
recommendation: Implement strict API rate-limiting middleware (such as express-rate-limit) to restrict the number of login requests an individual IP address can perform within a fixed timeframe. Additionally, enforce automated lockouts or multi-factor CAPTCHA prompts following successive authorization failures, and log anomalous credential validation bursts to automated alerting pipelines.

title: Missing Server-Side Object Integrity Checks During Profile Parameter Modification
category: A08 - Software or Data Integrity Failures
description: The application lets clients submit user-state attributes directly to profile routing handlers. Because the back-end system processes incoming text parameters directly from the browser context without evaluating digital signatures or verifying structural object boundaries, client-side actions can bypass standard execution limitations.
impact: Attackers can manually submit privileged parameter modifications inside intercepted HTTP requests using proxy tools like Burp Suite. This breaks data integrity baselines, allowing malicious actors to override structural data records or adjust local application context right from client runtime environments.
recommendation: Enforce strict server-side schema verification policies on all incoming request objects. Ensure data integrity parameters are fully recalculated and validated against trusted baseline models on the back-end controller layer before updating system database records.

title: Exposure of Sensitive Authentication Tokens in Plaintext API Responses
description: The application's authentication module transmits highly sensitive JSON Web Tokens (JWT) inside the raw HTTP response body upon a successful login event. Because the platform relies on cleartext transmissions and does not isolate or cryptographically mask active authorization signatures from the network layer, anyone sniffing local traffic can easily extract user identity hashes.
impact: An attacker capable of intercepting local network traffic can capture the exposed session tokens directly from the API response payload. Because the server returns full administrative bearer keys globally without transport-layer security or structural payload encryption, this leads to immediate session hijacking and complete administrative takeover without knowing the target's original cleartext password.
recommendation: Enforce strict Transport Layer Security (TLS/HTTPS) across all API endpoints to protect token transactions over the wire. Additionally, secure session tokens by using HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags rather than returning raw JWT strings inside the JSON response body, preventing frontend scripts or traffic sniffers from exposing the active signature.

title: Improper Input Validation Leading to Third-Party Dependency Disclosure
description: The application's file-server module enforces a restriction policy intended to limit public asset downloads strictly to '.md' and '.pdf' extensions. However, the sanitation filter can be completely bypassed by embedding an encoded null byte character sequence into the path string, tricking the backend router into delivering sensitive internal deployment configuration metrics.
impact: An attacker can download and audit internal software manifest files anonymously. This allows the attacker to cross-reference the application's entire dependency tree and version history with public vulnerability databases, paving the way for targeted supply-chain exploits against unpatched third-party packages.
recommendation: Refactor path validation filters on the backend to avoid processing legacy null terminator indicators. Ensure file extensions are whitelisted using a strong regex match or standard platform routing frameworks rather than basic suffix evaluation checks.

title: Sensitive Information Disclosure via Publicly Accessible FTP Directory
description: The application's underlying server architecture configuration leaves directory browsing enabled on specific local file path directories. An unauthenticated remote attacker can access the hidden path root directly via a standard browser session to actively view, download, and analyze raw directory structures and internal configuration layout files.
impact: This misconfiguration results in critical infrastructure layout and asset exposure. Anonymous users can pull system backups, dependency blueprints, and confidential data storage sheets (such as package maps or markdown logs), expanding the system attack surface for secondary environment penetration threats.
recommendation: Explicitly disable folder list permissions globally across all production web server profiles and container instances. Ensure that structural asset repositories are placed behind strong boundary access filters that demand valid authentication keys to query backend resources.

title: DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Global Search Bar
description: The global search functionality fails to sanitize user-supplied input parameters before rendering them back in the client-side DOM profile context. An attacker can manipulate the search query string 'q' to inject payload scripts, bypassing local application input validation.
impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript code within the context of a victim's active browser session. This can lead to unauthorized session hijacking, theft of active session cookies, manipulation of page layouts, or capturing sensitive credentials via fake login overlays.
recommendation: Implement strict context-aware output encoding using secure sanitization libraries such as DOMPurify before dynamically inserting user data into the webpage DOM. Additionally, enforce a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) header response layout to block unauthorized script execution.

title: Negative Quantity Accepted in Shopping Cart
description: The application accepts negative values for the product quantity. A request containing quantity: -1 was processed successfully by the server instead of being rejected, indicating insufficient enforcement of business rules and server-side validation.
impact: An attacker may manipulate shopping-cart quantities and pricing logic, resulting in invalid order values, negative totals, or abuse of the application's purchase workflow.
recommendation: Implement server-side validation to ensure product quantity is a positive integer within an allowed range. Reject zero, negative, non-numeric, and excessively large values before processing the request.

title: Business Logic Flaw – Negative Product Quantity Accepted
description: The application fails to enforce valid quantity rules on the server side. By modifying the basket quantity request in Burp Repeater, a negative quantity (-1) was accepted and stored successfully.
impact: An attacker may manipulate shopping-cart quantities and pricing logic, resulting in invalid order values, negative totals, or abuse of the application's purchase workflow.
recommendation: Implement strict server-side validation for basket quantities. Only positive integer values within an approved range should be accepted. Invalid or negative quantities should return an appropriate error such as 400 Bad Request.

title: Session Security Weakness – Authentication Token Remains Valid After Logout
description: The application does not properly invalidate the authentication token after logout. A previously captured Bearer token remained valid and continued to access the authenticated /rest/user/whoami endpoint after the user logged out.
impact: If an authentication token is stolen or exposed, it may remain usable even after the legitimate user logs out. This could allow continued unauthorized access to authenticated functionality until the token expires.
recommendation: Invalidate authentication tokens when a user logs out. Implement server-side token revocation or a token denylist, use short-lived access tokens, securely manage refresh tokens, and verify token validity on every authenticated request.

title: Authentication Flow Verified
description: Valid test credentials were submitted to the login endpoint. The server returned HTTP 200 OK and issued an authentication token, confirming successful authentication.
impact: Burp Suite Repeater response showing HTTP/1.1 200 OK and authentication token.
recommendation: Continue testing token handling, logout invalidation, session expiration, and access control before determining whether an authentication or session vulnerability exists.

title: Unauthorized Access to Another User's Basket
description: The application allows an authenticated user to access another user's basket by modifying the basket identifier in the request URL. While authenticated as UserId 25, changing the request from /rest/basket/6 to /rest/basket/5 returned basket data belonging to UserId 16.
impact: An authenticated user may access resources belonging to other users by manipulating object identifiers. This may expose sensitive user information or allow unauthorized interaction with another user's data.
recommendation: Implement server-side object-level authorization checks for every protected resource. Before returning a basket, the application should verify that the authenticated user's identity matches the owner of the requested basket.

title: Authentication Token Remains Valid After Logout
description: After logging out of the application, a previously issued JWT authentication token remained valid. The old token was replayed using Burp Suite Repeater in the Authorization: Bearer header and the server continued to return authenticated basket data.
impact: If an authentication token is obtained before logout, it may continue to authorize requests until the token expires. Logging out therefore does not immediately prevent reuse of a previously captured token.
recommendation: Implement effective session invalidation on logout. Consider short-lived access tokens, token revocation or denylisting where appropriate, refresh-token rotation, and server-side controls that prevent reuse of invalidated authentication sessions.

title: Authentication Token Cookie Missing HttpOnly Flag
description: The authentication token is stored in a browser cookie without the HttpOnly attribute. Testing with document.cookie confirmed that client-side JavaScript can access the token cookie.
impact: If a Cross-Site Scripting vulnerability is present, malicious JavaScript may be able to read the authentication token and increase the risk of session compromise.
recommendation: Store sensitive authentication cookies with the HttpOnly attribute enabled so that client-side JavaScript cannot directly access them. Additional protections such as Secure and an appropriate SameSite policy should also be evaluated for production deployment.

title: Missing Content Security Policy Header
description: The HTTP response for the OWASP Juice Shop main page does not include a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header.
impact: Without a Content Security Policy, the browser has fewer restrictions on which client-side resources can execute. This may increase the impact of client-side vulnerabilities such as Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
recommendation: Implement an appropriate Content-Security-Policy header that restricts scripts, styles, frames and other resources to trusted sources.
